Life Aboard: Ritual and Routine

Finding a ritual that works for you can change your entire approach to boating.
  • By Bob Arrington
  • September 3, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 5:13
Instaread

There’s a rhythm to life aboard that’s shaped not only by tides and weather but by the quiet sequences we enact each time we leave a harbor or return to one. These moments are not dramatic. They are a simple ritual my wife Dori and I share with each other. But they are essential to our life on board. They remind us that our voyages are not just about distance—they are about transformation.

It would be easy to call these routines. Many boaters do. We talk about the importance of routines aboard—departure routines, arrival routines, safety routines. And there is value in that language, but I’ve also come to believe there’s a danger in it. A routine, to me, is something you grow into doing mindlessly. It’s efficient and repeatable—but it requires very little presence. You brush your teeth. You tie your shoes. You go through the motions, barely thinking about them. 

A ritual is something else entirely. A ritual is done mindfully. It is chosen. It requires attention. Where a routine allows the mind to drift, a ritual calls it back. And out here, on the water, that distinction matters more than it might seem.

Most of the mistakes I’ve made handling our boat have occurred when a ritual has been interrupted. Our departure is a good example. Leaving a harbor is never just about lifting the anchor or releasing the lines. Before we go, Dori and I walk the decks, checking systems and reviewing departure lists. On the surface it looks routine—and in some ways it is. But if we let it become automatic or allow ourselves to become distracted, we lose something important. Because no two departures are ever really the same. Each requires our full presence. 

There’s also something else happening in those moments. We’re taking an inventory—not just of the boat, but of ourselves. What have we settled into during our stay? What are we carrying with us? What are we willing to leave behind?

There’s a moment, just before the engine turns over, when everything is still. The boat is quiet. The lines are ready to be released, or the anchor is ready to be lifted, when nothing has quite begun. That pause has become sacred to us. It’s the breath before the leap.

It would be easy to rush past it. To move straight from preparation to motion. But we’ve learned not to. Whether we’ve stayed a day or a month, departure always feels like a kind of shedding—a reset. A chance to begin again, not just in geography, but in mindset.

Even the mechanical tasks—checking oil levels, topping off water tanks, securing lockers—take on a different weight when approached as a ritual rather than routine. They are no longer just chores to be completed. They are affirmations. We are preparing ourselves as much as the vessel. We are choosing awareness over habit. 

Repetition invites efficiency. Familiarity invites shortcuts.

Once underway, that mindset carries forward. The boat becomes its own world, suspended between places. We settle into our roles—Dori at the helm, me monitoring systems and navigation—but even those roles can slip into routine if we’re not careful. The danger isn’t in repetition. It’s in disengagement, and the water doesn’t tolerate that for long.

Conditions change. Traffic appears where there was none. A shift in wind or current asks for attention. When we stay present, these are not interruptions—they are invitations. Each adjustment, each decision, keeps us connected to what’s happening in real time.

Underway, we often fall into a quiet rhythm. Conversation fades. The hum of the engine, the movement of the water, they all settle into the background. It would be easy, in that space, to drift mentally as well. But that’s where ritual matters most, because we are in between. No longer where we were, not yet where we’re going. It’s a liminal space, and it has a way of sharpening thought—if we allow it. Presence turns that in-between time into something meaningful. Without it, we simply pass through.

Arrival brings another opportunity. Pulling into a new harbor, we scan for landmarks, read the water, choose our spot. Dropping anchor or docking is both a technical act and a symbolic one. It says: We are here. If arrival becomes routine, it’s just another box checked. Lines secured. Engines off. Done. As a ritual, it becomes something more. 

After the boat is settled we try not to rush to get off the boat. We let the place come to us. That pause matters. It creates a transition—not just from movement to stillness, but from one experience to the next. It allows us to arrive, not just physically, but mentally. There’s a kind of reverence in that. An openness to whatever comes next. Sometimes it’s exploration. Sometimes it’s conversation with other cruisers. Sometimes it’s simply a quiet evening aboard.

The rituals follow a simple pattern—we prepare, we move, we arrive. And in doing so, we remain connected—not just to the mechanics of the journey, but to its meaning. Cruising isn’t just about where we go. It’s about how we go.

This article originally appeared in the September 2026 issue of Power & Motoryacht magazine.
